questions.q: State the fundamental difference between a mechanical finish and a chemical finish in terms of the mechanism of action on the fabric.
questions.a: Mechanical finishes use physical forces (heat, pressure, friction, tension) to alter fabric surface/structure without chemical reaction; chemical finishes apply chemical agents that bond with fibres or form a polymer film to impart new properties. A wrong answer (e.g., "mechanical finishes use machines, chemical finishes use chemicals") reveals confusion between equipment and mechanism — sanforizing uses a machine but works by controlled compressive shrinkage (physical), while a softener applied by the same padding mangle works by chemical lubrication.

questions.q: A cotton fabric is passed through heated rollers under high pressure to produce a high-gloss surface. Identify the finish, classify it, and explain why the gloss may disappear after washing.
questions.a: The finish is calendaring (specifically friction calendaring) — a mechanical finish. The gloss is produced by flattening fibres and fusing surface fibres under heat/pressure; it is not chemically bonded, so laundering restores fibre mobility and the gloss fades. A student who says "the chemical wears off" misclassifies it as chemical and misunderstands the physical nature of the surface modification.

questions.q: A manufacturer wants to prevent a cotton shirting fabric from shrinking more than 1% after repeated home laundering. Which mechanical finish should be applied, and what is the principle behind it?
questions.a: Sanforizing (compressive shrinkage). The fabric is fed through a rubber blanket stretched over a steam-heated cylinder; when the blanket contracts, it compresses the fabric, forcing yarns closer and removing residual shrinkage potential. A student suggesting "calendaring" confuses surface gloss with dimensional stability; calendaring does not guarantee residual shrinkage control.

questions.q: Compare the durability of a fluorocarbon-based water-repellent finish and a wax-based water-repellent finish on a polyester-cotton blend. Which will withstand more launderings and why?
questions.a: Fluorocarbon finish is more durable. Fluoropolymers form covalent bonds with fibre surfaces and have low surface energy that resists surfactant penetration during washing; wax finishes are merely deposited on the surface and are removed by detergents and mechanical action. A student claiming "both are chemical so both are durable" misses the critical distinction between reactive (durable) and non-reactive (temporary) chemical finishes.

questions.q: Evaluate the suitability of a formaldehyde-based resin wrinkle-resistant finish for children's sleepwear considering current safety regulations and consumer preferences. Propose an alternative.
questions.a: Unsuitable. Formaldehyde resins release free formaldehyde, a known carcinogen and skin irritant, which is restricted by FSSAI/BIS standards for children's wear. Alternative: formaldehyde-free resin (e.g., DMDHEU with blocked isocyanate) or butanetetracarboxylic acid (BTCA) — a polycarboxylic acid cross-linker that provides durable press with low formaldehyde release. A student recommending "no finish" ignores the functional need for wrinkle resistance; the competency is balancing performance with safety.

questions.q: Design a finish sequence for a 100% cotton fabric intended for premium summer shirting that must have: (a) soft handle, (b) low shrinkage, (c) wrinkle resistance, (d) soil release. Specify mechanical/chemical, order, and justify each step.
questions.a: 1. Singeing (mechanical) — remove protruding fibres for smooth surface. 2. Desizing/scouring/bleaching (wet prep) — not finishes but essential prep. 3. Sanforizing (mechanical) — compressive shrinkage control before resin to avoid distortion. 4. Pad-dry-cure with DMDHEU resin + catalyst + softener (chemical) — imparts wrinkle resistance and soft handle simultaneously. 5. Fluorocarbon soil-release agent applied in same bath or separate pad (chemical) — durable soil release. Order matters: mechanical shrinkage control before resin curing; softener and soil-release must be compatible with resin (non-ionic softener). A student putting softener before resin would get poor cross-linking; putting sanforizing after resin would distort the cured fabric.
